tables.description: Summary statistics: number of unique firms, firm-month observations, and distribution of firm lifetimes (months in sample) for each of the 14 countries, January 1985-June 2006.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves correct universe construction and data ingestion: country assignment (14 non-U.S. markets), sample period (258 months), inclusion of delisted firms (survivorship-free), and correct monthly panel assembly. Because the replication substitutes Compustat Global + Compustat NA (Canada) for the paper's proprietary FactSet vintage, absolute counts are evaluated at the pattern level (Tier 2): Japan and UK must be the largest markets, Austria/Norway among the smallest, and total firm-month observations must be of the same order (~2.4M in the paper).
tables.paper_quote: Table 1 reports some diagnostics of each country included in the sample: the number of unique firms, the number of firm-month observations, and the distribution of the number of months that firms exist in the sample. The sample includes stocks from Austria, Belgium, Canada, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and United Kingdom for the time period January 1985–June 2006 (258 months). (L59)
tables.notes: Data-substitution table: counts cannot match FactSet exactly; evaluated at Tier 2 (cross-country magnitude pattern). Tolerance set at 50% per count-type default.

tables.description: Time-series averages of monthly cross-sectional regression return responses (country-dummy intercepts) at lags 1-12 and every 12th lag through 60, for OLS (all countries, Europe, Canada, Japan) and heteroskedasticity-adjusted WLS (all countries, Europe), February 1985-June 2006.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves the cross-sectional regression methodology: monthly univariate regressions of r_{i,t} on a single lagged return r_{i,t-k} with 14 country dummies, time-series averaging of gamma_{k,t}, OLS and WLS (weights = reciprocal of pooled country return variance), and the four sample splits. Reproducing the lag profile — strong negative lag-1 reversal (~-0.029), positive responses at annual lags 12/24/36/48/60 (~0.015/0.006/0.008/0.007/0.009) — validates the monthly return computation, lag indexing, and country-neutralization at once.
tables.paper_quote: monthly univariate cross-sectional regressions of the form r_{i,t} = alpha_{k,t} + gamma_{k,t} r_{i,t-k} + u_{i,t} are calculated for each month t and lag k ... The regression is calculated for every month t from February 1985 through June 2006 (257 months), and for lag k values 1–12, and each 12th lag thereafter through 60. Regression results (using country dummy variables for intercept) are reported separately for different samples: all countries, European countries only, Canada, and Japan. The time-series averages of gamma_{k,t} as well as t-statistics are reported. (L122)

tables.description: Top-minus-bottom decile spread returns (EW and VW; Panel A sorts on returns in excess of country EW index, Panel B on total returns) for Year 1 / Years 2-3 / Years 4-5 annual, nonannual, difference, and all strategies, decomposed into total / intracountry / intercountry components, February 1985-June 2006.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves the core portfolio methodology of the paper: monthly decile sorts with equal number of stocks per bin, annual-lag (multiples of 12) vs nonannual-lag signal construction averaged within Year 1 / Years 2-3 / Years 4-5 windows, 1-month holding period with monthly rebalancing, EW and VW aggregation, and the intra/intercountry return decomposition. Reproducing the headline pattern — positive annual spreads (Y2-3 annual +0.0037, Y4-5 annual +0.0044 EW Panel A) against strongly negative nonannual spreads (Y2-3 nonannual -0.0143, Y4-5 nonannual -0.0056), difference > 1%/month — validates signal definition, sort mechanics, and country-EW benchmark construction simultaneously.
tables.paper_quote: Each month stocks are grouped into 10 portfolios (with equal number of stocks in each portfolio) based on past performance. For example, the trading strategy that is formed based on past annual returns during Years 4–5 ranks stocks according to their average returns during the historical lags 48 and 60. For each strategy, Table 3 reports the portfolio return spread of the top-minus-bottom decile. The difference strategy is the annual strategy minus the nonannual strategy. (L234)

tables.description: Top-minus-bottom EW decile spread returns of the annual / nonannual / difference / all strategies computed separately within each of the 14 countries, February 1985-June 2006.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves the international breadth of the pattern: the annual-vs-nonannual spread must hold country-by-country (positive Y2-3 and Y4-5 annual-minus-nonannual differences in nearly all 14 countries, e.g. +0.0198 Canada, +0.0156 Japan, +0.0158 France), not merely in the pooled cross-section dominated by Japan/UK. This exercises per-country sort grouping and validates that the country-EW benchmark and decile construction are applied correctly within each market.
tables.paper_quote: In Table 7, each month stocks are grouped into 10 portfolios (with equal number of stocks in each portfolio) based on their past performance relative to their country equal-weighted average. ... The average monthly returns of the various trading strategies are reported separately for each country in the sample for the period February 1985–June 2006 (257 months). (L1498)

tables.description: EW Panel-A decile spreads (annual/nonannual/difference/all for Year 1, Years 2-3, Years 4-5) reported separately for each calendar month Jan-Dec plus Feb-Dec, February 1985-June 2006.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves the annual pattern is NOT a January/turn-of-year effect: annual spreads are positive in nearly every calendar month, Years 2-3/4-5 nonannual spreads are negative in most months, and the Feb-Dec column remains significant (paper pp. 1141-1143, L1178-1182). Exercises the calendar-month decomposition of the decile-spread time series — a distinct check from the pooled averages in Table 3.
tables.paper_quote: the average monthly returns of the various trading strategies are reported separately for every calendar month during the period February 1985–June 2006 (257 months). ... In a separate column, returns are computed using all non-January months. (L740)

tables.description: EW Panel-A decile spreads within 30/40/30 USD market-cap size groups (small/medium/large), using intracountry and intercountry size breakpoints, re-evaluated monthly; Year 1 / Years 2-3 / Years 4-5 panels.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves the pattern is not a microcap/illiquidity artifact: annual-vs-nonannual differences persist across small, medium, and large stocks under both domestic and global size definitions (paper Section IV.A, L1200-1204). Exercises size-conditional sorting with monthly-reformed breakpoints (Table-5-specific convention) — distinct from Tables 3/7 which pool all sizes.
tables.paper_quote: Table 5 reports the results of this procedure, performed separately for 3 different size groups (measured by market capitalization in U.S. dollars), within each country and across all countries. Small firms are defined as the bottom 30%, large firms are the top 30%, and the remaining 40% are medium-size firms. The size categorization is reevaluated in the beginning of every month. (L1218)

tables.description: Pairwise correlations across countries of the monthly annual-strategy (EW Panel-A annual decile spread) return series, in three panels (Year 1, Years 2-3, Years 4-5), plus the text's reported extremes and 5% significance threshold.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves the strategies are not highly correlated across countries — the paper's evidence against a pervasive global-risk explanation (abstract L11; Section IV.B L3105, L3599): Year-1 annual correlations are partly significant (France-Germany 0.43, France-UK 0.34), but longer-horizon annual-strategy correlations range from -0.19 to +0.20 with a preponderance insignificant (5% level 0.12). Exercises the independence of the 14 per-country strategy series computed for Table 7.
tables.paper_quote: The correlation reaches as high as 43% between France and Germany, and 34% between France and the United Kingdom. But many of the correlations are small and statistically insignificant. The longer-term annual strategies have lower correlations across countries, ranging from -19% (Years 4–5 annual strategy correlation between Switzerland and Austria) to 20% (Years 2–3 annual strategy correlation between Sweden and France). (L3105, L3599)
tables.notes: Committed metrics are the paper's explicitly reported cells (named pairs, extremes, significance threshold). The full 14x14 correlation matrices per panel are reported in results/table_11_correlations.md as supplementary statistics.

tables.description: EW Panel-A-style strategy returns for quintile (5 bins; Q1..Q5 and 5-1 spread) and tricile (3 bins; T1..T3 and 3-1 spread) sorts, for annual/nonannual/difference/all rows in the three year-group panels.
tables.replication_meaning: Proves robustness to bin count: quintile and tricile top-minus-bottom spreads keep the decile sign pattern (negative nonannual and positive annual difference rows at Years 2-3/4-5; paper Section IV.D, L3601-3603). Exercises the sort mechanics at alternative granularities — distinct from the decile-only Tables 3/7.
tables.paper_quote: To address the robustness of the decile methodology, Table 12 reports average returns to quintile and tricile strategies. The quintile and tricile spreads are returns of the top 5th or 3rd of stocks, respectively, in excess of the bottom 5th (L3603)
